newsitem.title: UK: Insurers pay 50 mln stg for secure e-mail system.
newsitem.headline: Insurers pay 50 mln stg for secure e-mail system.

text.p: The world's top four insurance brokers have so far ploughed around 50 million stg into the World Insurance Network (WIN) communications system, WIN's chairman said at its launch on Tuesday.
Total costs in the three years the project has taken to come to fruition were hard to gauge, but were approaching 50 million stg, outgoing chairman Denis Mahoney told a news conference.
Direct costs were 13 million stg, but indirect costs such as the loan of personnel by the backers -- Marsh & McLennan, Aon Corp, Willis Corroon and Sedgwick -- were hard to judge.

The WINconnect service launched today offers a secure, global communications service to subscribers in the insurance community and a directory of brokers and insurers, which will eventually expand to between 300,000 and 500,000 entries.

Incoming chairman Ron Forrest said future developments would make WIN more interesting, but noted that its current email function should not be under-estimated as some industry players do not currently have access to such links.
The aims of WIN are to improve efficiency and reduce costs in the insurance industry, where brokers in particular have been squeezed by tough market conditions in recent years.
David Norris Jones, chairman of Sedgwick Risk Services, said, "As an industry, we are one of the most inefficient service providers you will find...WIN will enable us to get up to date very quickly."
Future plans for WIN, which is based in London, include the addition of news and information services and WINvoice, "a community voice transmission service" WIN said in a statement.
WIN said it will have more than 30 corporate users signed up around the world by the year end.
Representatives from companies involved in testing WINconnect were enthusiastic about its potential.
Rick Hudson of Royal & Sun Alliance said it would cut costs, speed up business processes and would also allow insurers to talk directly to their reinsurers without having to go through their brokers.
A spokesman for the Lloyd's market Brockbank group said the service would prove invaluable to organisations like his which conduct most of their business abroad.
He cited the UK direct telephone insurer Direct Line as an example of how the use of technology could transform the industry and slash costs.
WIN's own research suggests that a move towards electronic documents and away from paper can lead to huge savings in couriers, faxes and telephone costs.
"WIN is just the starting point, but can already deliver huge benefits," said Mahoney, who described the industry's current paper based transaction systems "as medieval at best."
Joint chief executive Richard Wales said the aim was to make WIN the preferred electronic market place of the future which will promote the adoption of international standards.
WIN is working with other electronic networks in the insurance world, Forrest said, adding that it was not competing with them but complemented them.
However, uncertainty has dogged the development of electronic systems in the insurance world following the slow take-up of London based LIMNET (London Market Insurance Network) in recent years.
LIMNET is one of the organisations working with WIN on developing joint standards.
WIN has been developed in co-operation with British Telecommunications Plc, supported by Control Data, Hewlett Packard and Andersen Consulting.
-- John Sanders, Reuters Insurance News +44 171 642 2769
